{{Short description|Lower bound for bandit problem}}
The '''Lai–Robbins lower bound'''<ref name="Lai1985"/> gives an asymptotic lower bound on the regret that any uniformly good algorithm must incur in the stochastic [[Multi-armed bandit|multi-armed bandit problem]]. The original result was proved by [[Tze Leung Lai]] and [[Herbert Robbins]] in 1985 for parametric [[Exponential family|exponential families]]. Later work extended the statement to more general classes of distributions.<ref name="Maillard2019"/>

== Multi-armed bandit problem ==

The [[Multi-armed bandit|multi-armed bandit problem]] (MAB) is a [[sequential game]] in which the player must trade off exploration (to learn) and exploitation (to earn).

The player chooses among <math>K</math> actions (arms) with unknown distributions <math>\nu = (\nu_1,\dots,\nu_K)</math>. The player is assumed to know a class of distributions <math>\mathcal{D}</math> such that for every <math>k</math> one has <math>\nu_k\in\mathcal{D}</math> (for example, <math>\mathcal{D}</math> may be the family of [[Normal distribution|Gaussian]] or [[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]] distributions).

At each round <math>t=1,\dots,T</math> the player selects (pulls) an arm <math>a_t</math> and observes a reward <math>X_t\sim\nu_{a_t}</math>.

We denote
* <math>N_a(t):=\sum_{s=1}^t\mathbf{1}_{\{a_s=a\}}</math> the number of times arm <math>a</math> has been pulled in the first <math>t</math> rounds,
* <math>\mu(\nu):=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K)</math> the vector of arm means, where <math>\mu_k=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\nu_k}[X]</math>,
* <math>\mu^*:=\max_a \mu_a</math> the highest mean 
* <math>\Delta_a:=\mu^*-\mu_a\ge 0</math> the gap of arm <math>a</math>.

An arm <math>a</math> with <math>\mu_a=\mu^*</math> is called an '''optimal arm'''; otherwise it is a '''suboptimal arm'''.

The goal is to '''minimize the regret''' at horizon <math>T</math>, defined by
:<math>R_T:= \sum_{a=1}^K \Delta_a\,\mathbb{E}[N_a(T)].</math>

Intuitively, the regret is the (expected) total loss compared to always playing an optimal arm:
:<math>\text{regret}=\sum_{a}\ (\text{cost of playing }a)\times(\text{times }a\text{ is played}).</math>

An MAB algorithm is a (possibly randomized) policy that, at each round <math>t</math>, choose an arm a_t by using the observations received from previous turns.<ref name="Lattimore"/>

=== Intuitive example ===
Suppose a farmer must choose, each year, one of <math>K</math> seed varieties to plant. Each variety <math>k</math> has an unknown average yield <math>\mu_k</math>. If the farmer knew the best variety (with mean <math>\mu^*</math>) he would plant it every year; in reality he must try varieties to learn which is best. The cumulative regret after <math>T</math> years measures the total expected loss in yield due to imperfect knowledge.

'''Remarks'''
# The model above is the ''stochastic'' MAB; there also exist adversarial variants.<ref name="Lattimore"/>
# One may consider a ''fixed-horizon'' setting (known <math>T</math>) or an ''anytime'' setting (unknown <math>T</math>).

== Lai–Robbins lower bound ==

The theorem gives the right amount of time we should pull a suboptimal arm <math>k</math> to distinguish whether we are in the instance with <math>\nu_k</math> or with <math>\tilde{\nu}_k</math> where <math>\tilde{\nu}_k</math> is such that <math>\tilde{\mu}_k > \mu^*</math>.

Knowning a lower bound on the number of pull of every suboptimal arm gives a lower bound on the regret as only suboptimal arms contribute to the regret.

Before stating the formal theorem we need to define what is a consistent algorithm.

=== Consistency (uniformly good algorithms) ===

Let <math>\mathcal{D}</math> be a class of probability distributions and consider <math>K</math> arms with reward distributions
<math>\nu = (\nu_1,\dots,\nu_K) \in \mathcal{D}^K</math>.
An algorithm is said to be ''consistent'' (also called ''uniformly good'') on <math>\mathcal{D}^K</math> if, for every instance <math>\nu \in \mathcal{D}^K</math>, the expected regret <math>R_T(\nu)</math> grows subpolynomially:
:<math>\forall \alpha > 0, \qquad
R_T(\nu) = o(T^\alpha)
\quad \text{as } T \to \infty</math>

This assumption excludes algorithms that perform well on some instances but incur linear regret on others.

=== Formal lower bound ===

For any suboptimal arm <math>a</math>.
For a distribution <math>\nu_a \in \mathcal{D}</math> and a threshold <math>x</math>, define
:<math>\mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\nu_a, x, \mathcal{D})
:= \inf \Bigl\{
\operatorname{KL}(\nu_a, \nu') :
\nu' \in \mathcal{D},
\ \mu' > x
\Bigr\}</math>
where <math>\operatorname{KL}(\cdot,\cdot)</math> denotes the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence|Kullback-Leibler divergence]].

Then, for any algorithm consistent on <math>\mathcal{D}^K</math> and for every instance
<math>\nu \in \mathcal{D}^K</math>, every suboptimal arm <math>a</math> satisfies
:<math>\mathbb{E}_\nu[N_a(T)]
\ge
\frac{\ln T}{\mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\nu_a, \mu^*, \mathcal{D})}
+ o(\ln T)</math>

Consequently, the regret satisfies
:<math>R_T(\nu)
\ge
\left(
\sum_{a:\,\mu_a < \mu^*}
\frac{\Delta_a}{\mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\nu_a, \mu^*, \mathcal{D})}
\right)
\ln T
+ o(\ln T)</math>

The original 1985 paper<ref name="Lai1985"/> established this result for exponential families; later work showed that the bound holds under much weaker assumptions on <math>\mathcal{D}</math>.

=== Intuition  ===

Consistency imposes that, for every <math>\nu</math>, the number of pulls of an optimal arm must be large. This means that <math>\mu^*</math> is estimated very accurately. The goal is to determine, for a suboptimal arm <math>k</math>, how many samples are needed to be confident, with the appropriate level of confidence, that <math>\mu_k < \mu^*</math>. To do so, we use what is called the '''most confusing instance''': an instance close to <math>\nu</math> such that arm <math>k</math> is optimal. We define it as <math>\tilde{\nu}</math> such that, for all <math>a \neq k</math>, <math>\tilde{\nu}_a = \nu_a</math>, and <math>\tilde{\nu}_k</math> is chosen so that <math>\tilde{\mu}_k > \mu^*</math>. The objective is to determine how many samples of arm <math>k</math> are required to distinguish whether we are in the instance with <math>\nu_k</math> or with <math>\tilde{\nu}_k</math> in terms of <math>\operatorname{KL}</math> distance.

== Algorithms achieving the Lai–Robbins lower bound ==

Several algorithms are known to achieve the Lai–Robbins asymptotic lower bound
under specific assumptions on the reward distribution class <math>\mathcal{D}</math>.
The following list summarizes a non-exhaustive list of algorithms matching the lower bound.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Non-exhaustive list of algorithms achieving the lower bound under various distributional assumptions
! Distribution class <math>\mathcal{D}</math>
! Algorithms
|-
| Gaussian rewards (known variance)
| [[Kullback–Leibler Upper Confidence Bound|KL-UCB]],<ref name="Cappe2013"/> [[Thompson sampling|TS]],<ref name="Agrawal2012"/> AdaUCB,<ref name="Lattimore2018"/> RB-SDA<ref name="Baudry2020"/>
|-
| Gaussian rewards
| CHK<ref name="Cowan2018"/>
|-
| One-dimensional exponential families
| [[Kullback–Leibler Upper Confidence Bound|KL-UCB]]<ref name="Cappe2013"/>
|-
| Bounded rewards <math>\mathcal{P}([0,1])</math>
| [[Kullback–Leibler Upper Confidence Bound|KL-UCB]],<ref name="Cappe2013"/> [[Algorithm IMED|IMED]],<ref name="Honda2015"/> Fast-IMED,<ref name="Baudry2023"/> DMED,<ref name="Honda2010"/> NPTS,<ref name="Riou2020"/> KL-UCB-switch<ref name="Garivier2022"/>
|}

== Extension to other problems ==

=== Structured bandit ===

A more complexe is structured bandit where we know that the mean of each arm is in a set with some restriction. In this case we can prove a smaller lower bound that use the knowledge of this set.<ref name="Graves1997"/><ref name="Kaufmann2020"/>

=== Best arm identification (BAI) ===

A similar result has been proved for best arm identification, which is the same game except that, instead of minimizing the regret, the goal is to identify the best arm with probability <math>1 - \delta</math> using as few rounds as possible.<ref name="Garivier2016"/>

=== Reinforcement Learning (RL) ===

Similar results have been proved for regret minimization in average-reward reinforcement learning. The order is also <math>\ln T</math>, with a constant that depends on the problem.<ref name="Boone2025"/>
